title: git stash
definition: Temporarily shelves (or stashes) changes you've made to your working copy so you can work on something else, and then come back and re-apply them later.
simpleExplanation: The panic button. You are halfway through coding a feature when your boss yells 'EMERGENCY BUG ON MAIN BRANCH!'. You can't commit your feature because it's half-broken. You run `git stash`. Git scoops up all your messy desk papers and shoves them in a drawer, leaving you with a perfectly clean desk to fix the bug. Later, you run `git stash pop` to pull the papers back out of the drawer.
realWorldExample: Switching branches when you have dirty, uncommitted files in your Working Directory.
useCases: Cleaning the working directory without losing work

basic: What command puts your stashed files back into your Working Directory?
intermediate: Does `git stash` save brand new, untracked files?

answers.question: Untracked files?
answers.answer: By default, NO. If you created a brand new file, `git stash` will leave it sitting there. You must use `git stash -u` (include untracked) to stash everything.

codeExample:
# 1. You are coding, but need to switch branches urgently.
$ git stash
# Output: Saved working directory and index state WIP on main

# 2. Your working directory is now clean! Switch branches safely.
$ git checkout hotfix-branch

# ... fix the bug, commit it ...

# 3. Switch back to your feature branch.
$ git checkout main

# 4. Pull your messy code back out of the drawer!
$ git stash pop
